column9: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw rows of tiny empty boxes. He named them "cells" because they reminded him of what?
column14: Drops of water on a window
column15: Grains of sand on a beach
column16: Small, plain rooms like the ones monks lived in
column17: Seeds inside a fruit
column28: Hooke thought the boxes looked like the small rooms, or cells, where monks lived, so he named them cells. They were not seeds, sand, or water drops; they were the empty walls of dead plant cells.
column29: Where else do you hear the word cell used for a small space?

column9: Anton van Leeuwenhoek scraped the white film off his own teeth and looked at it through one of his homemade lenses. What did he discover?
column14: Grains of sugar from his food
column15: Nothing; the sample had no structure
column16: Dead cork cells
column17: Tiny living organisms that we now call bacteria
column28: Leeuwenhoek saw tiny moving organisms in the film from his teeth. They were bacteria, each one a single living cell. A common mistake is thinking cells were only found in plants, but Leeuwenhoek showed living single cells are all around us.
column29: The film on your teeth is full of something alive that brushing removes.

column9: Theodor Schwann studied tissues such as cartilage and nerve under the microscope. In 1839 he concluded that all ___ are made of cells.
column28: Schwann studied animal tissues and concluded that all animals are made of cells. Schleiden had already said the same about plants. A common mix-up is switching the two: Schleiden = plants, Schwann = animals.
column29: Schleiden had already shown this for plants. Schwann looked at the other big group of many-celled organisms.

column9: One scientist summed up an idea with the Latin phrase omnis cellula e cellula, which means "every cell from a cell." Which part of the cell theory does this phrase describe?
column14: All living things are made of one or more cells
column15: All cells come from pre-existing cells
column16: All cells have a similar chemical makeup
column17: Cells are the basic unit of structure and function
column28: "Every cell from a cell" means new cells only come from cells that already exist. That was Rudolf Virchow's idea in 1855. The other choices are true parts of the cell theory, but they are not what this phrase says.
column29: Focus on the word from. The phrase tells where cells come from.

column9: The modern cell theory says cells contain genetic information that is passed on when they divide. Which molecule holds this information?
column14: Salt
column15: Water
column16: DNA
column17: Glucose
column28: DNA holds a cell's genetic instructions and is copied when the cell divides. Glucose is a sugar used for energy, and water and salt do not carry instructions.
column29: It is the nucleic acid from Unit 2 that carries the code for traits.

column9: According to the cell theory, new cells can form from nonliving material such as dust or mud.
column28: False. The cell theory says all cells come from pre-existing cells. The old idea that life forms from nonliving material is called spontaneous generation, and experiments disproved it.
column29: Where does the cell theory say every new cell comes from?

column9: A bean plant grows from 10 cm to 30 cm tall in a few weeks. Where did the new cells in its stem come from?
column14: Sunlight that formed into cells
column15: Existing plant cells that divided
column16: Soil that turned into plant cells
column17: Water that changed into cells
column28: The plant grows because its existing cells divide to make new cells. Soil, water, and sunlight supply materials and energy, but they do not turn into cells. A common mistake is thinking the plant is made directly from soil.
column29: The cell theory says every new cell comes from a cell that was already there.

column9: What process makes two new cells from one existing cell?
column14: Evaporation
column15: Spontaneous generation
column16: Cell division
column17: Melting
column28: In cell division, one parent cell splits into two new cells. Spontaneous generation is the disproven idea that life comes from nonliving things, and melting and evaporation are changes of state, not life processes.
column29: Think about what your body does to make new skin after a scrape.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: A student says, "Mushrooms aren't plants or animals, so the cell theory doesn't apply to them." Which response is correct?
column14: She is right; the cell theory was written only for plants and animals, so fungi are left out.
column15: She is wrong; mushrooms are actually a kind of animal, so the theory covers them.
column16: She is right; mushrooms are made of minerals from the soil, not cells.
column17: She is wrong; the cell theory applies to all living things, including fungi like mushrooms.
column28: The cell theory applies to every living thing: plants, animals, fungi, protists, and bacteria. The first evidence came from plants and animals, but later scientists found cells in all life. Mushrooms are fungi, not animals.
column29: Does the cell theory say SOME living things or ALL living things are made of cells?

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Which of these are made of one or more cells? Select all that apply.
column14: A bacterium on your skin
column15: A raindrop
column16: A housefly
column17: An oak tree
column28: Oak trees, yeast, houseflies, and bacteria are living things, so each is made of one or more cells. Sand and raindrops are nonliving and have no cells. Don't skip the tiny one-celled organisms; they count too.
column29: Pick only the things that are alive, even the tiny ones.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: How many cells make up one bacterium, such as E. coli?
column14: Two
column15: Several thousand
column16: None; bacteria are not made of cells
column17: Exactly one
column28: A bacterium is a single cell, so it is unicellular. A common mistake is choosing none because bacteria are so small, but every bacterium is a complete living cell.
column29: Bacteria are the classic example of a unicellular organism.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: The blue whale is the largest animal on Earth. What does the cell theory tell us about its body?
column14: It is made of a huge number of cells.
column15: Only its organs are made of cells; its blubber is not.
column16: It is too large to be made of cells.
column17: It is one giant cell.
column28: All living things are made of cells, and large organisms are made of enormous numbers of them. Size does not change the rule. Even blubber is a tissue made of fat cells.
column29: The cell theory has no size limit. What must even a giant animal be built from?

column9: Which kind of large molecule is found in every cell, from a bacterium to a human nerve cell?
column14: Hemoglobin
column15: Proteins
column16: Chlorophyll
column17: Cellulose
column28: Every cell uses proteins to build structures and run reactions, which is part of why the cell theory says all cells have a similar chemical makeup. Cellulose is in plant cell walls, chlorophyll is only in cells that photosynthesize, and hemoglobin is in red blood cells, so none of those is in every cell.
column29: Pick the general class of macromolecule, not one specific molecule that only certain cells make.

column9: Which element is found in every living cell?
column14: Gold
column15: Carbon
column16: Helium
column17: Neon
column28: Carbon is the backbone of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, so every cell contains it. Cells do not use gold, and neon and helium are noble gases that do not form compounds in cells.
column29: Think of CHNOPS from Unit 2.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Which part of the cell theory says that the things a living thing does, like digesting food or moving, are carried out by its cells?
column14: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column15: Cells can form from nonliving matter.
column16: All cells have a similar chemical makeup.
column17: Cells are the basic unit of structure and function.
column28: Function means the jobs that get done. The cell is the basic unit of function because life's jobs happen in cells. "Cells can form from nonliving matter" is not part of the cell theory at all.
column29: Look for the statement with a word that means the job something does.

column9: Match each scientist to his contribution to the cell theory.
column14: Robert Hooke :: Named cells after looking at cork
column15: Anton van Leeuwenhoek :: First saw living single-celled organisms
column16: Matthias Schleiden :: Concluded that all plants are made of cells
column17: Theodor Schwann :: Concluded that all animals are made of cells
column18: Rudolf Virchow :: Stated that all cells come from pre-existing cells
column28: Hooke named cells (cork, 1665). Leeuwenhoek first saw living single cells (1670s). Schleiden studied plants (1838) and Schwann studied animals (1839). Virchow said all cells come from cells (1855). The most common mix-up is switching Schleiden and Schwann.
column29: Start with the one you know best, like Hooke and cork, then work through the rest.

column9: Your skin sheds thousands of dead cells every day, yet you never run out of skin. Why?
column14: Dead skin cells come back to life.
column15: Dust settles on your body and becomes skin.
column16: Living skin cells divide to make new skin cells.
column17: Skin forms from the water you drink.
column28: Deeper, living skin cells keep dividing to replace the ones that flake off. That is the cell theory idea that all cells come from pre-existing cells. Water and dust do not turn into cells, and dead cells do not come back to life.
column29: New cells have to come from somewhere. What does the cell theory say they come from?

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Which organism is made of only one cell?
column14: Earthworm
column15: Frog
column16: Sunflower
column17: Amoeba
column28: An amoeba is a single cell that carries out every life process on its own. Earthworms, sunflowers, and frogs are multicellular, made of many cells.
column29: Three of these you can see easily without a microscope.

column9: When one cell divides, two new cells form. What are the two new cells called?
column14: Daughter cells
column15: Tissues
column16: Organelles
column17: Molecules
column28: The cell that divides is the parent cell, and the two new cells are daughter cells. Tissues are groups of many cells, organelles are parts inside a cell, and molecules are not alive.
column29: The new cells are named as if the old cell were their parent.

column9: A flu virus is much smaller than a cell and is not made of a cell. Can a flu virus make copies of itself on its own?
column14: No, it must get inside a living host cell to be copied.
column15: No, a virus can never be copied, even inside a living cell.
column16: Yes, it divides in two on its own, just like a bacterium does.
column17: Yes, it forms new copies from dust and moisture in the air.
column28: A virus is not a cell, so it cannot carry out life processes on its own. It has to invade a living cell and use that cell's parts to make copies. That is a big reason biologists using the cell theory do not call viruses living.
column29: A virus has no cell parts of its own to do the work.

column9: In which century did Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow put together the main ideas of the cell theory?
column14: The 2000s
column15: The 1800s
column16: The 1500s
column17: The 1600s
column28: Schleiden (1838), Schwann (1839), and Virchow (1855) all worked in the 1800s. A common mistake is picking the 1600s, which is when Hooke and Leeuwenhoek first saw cells, almost 200 years earlier.
column29: Cells were first seen in the 1600s, and the theory took a long time to come together after that.

column4: Cell theory as a scientific theory
column9: The cell theory is called a scientific theory. What does that mean?
column14: It is a fact that can never be changed.
column15: It is a well-tested explanation supported by a large amount of evidence.
column16: It is one scientist's personal opinion.
column17: It is a guess that has never been tested.
column28: A scientific theory is a broad explanation backed by lots of evidence from many scientists. It is not a guess or an opinion. Theories can still be updated with new evidence, which is how the modern cell theory added new ideas.
column29: In everyday talk, theory can mean a guess. In science it means something much stronger.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: A student puts a thin piece of an Elodea leaf under a microscope and sees many small, box-shaped units packed together, each filled with green dots. What is she looking at?
column14: Atoms
column15: Air bubbles
column16: Grains of sand
column17: Plant cells
column28: Each box is a plant cell, and the green dots are chloroplasts. Atoms are far too small to see with a light microscope. Finding cells in every leaf sample is evidence that living things are made of cells.
column29: Elodea is a living water plant. What are living things built from?

column9: Bakers add a small amount of yeast to bread dough. A few hours later, the dough holds far more yeast cells than were added. Where did the extra yeast cells come from?
column14: The original yeast cells divided to make new yeast cells.
column15: Heat from the kitchen created them.
column16: The flour turned into yeast.
column17: The sugar in the dough formed into cells.
column28: Yeast are single-celled fungi that reproduce by dividing (budding). The flour and sugar are food for the yeast, but they do not turn into cells. All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column29: Flour and sugar are food. What can make a new yeast cell?

column9: Which of these is NOT made of cells?
column14: A goldfish
column15: A pebble
column16: An ant
column17: A patch of moss
column28: A pebble is nonliving rock, so it has no cells. Goldfish, moss, and ants are all living things, so they are made of cells.
column29: Three of these are alive.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Which example best shows that cells are the basic unit of FUNCTION in living things?
column14: A drawing shows the shape of a cell.
column15: A stone wall is built from many stones.
column16: Salt crystals form in a dish of salt water.
column17: Nerve cells carry signals that let you feel a pinprick.
column28: Function means doing a job. Nerve cells doing the job of carrying signals shows that the work of life happens in cells. A stone wall and salt crystals are nonliving, and a drawing of a cell's shape is about structure, not function.
column29: Look for a living cell doing a job.

column9: The cell theory says all cells come from pre-existing cells. What does pre-existing mean?
column14: Not alive
column15: Already existing before
column16: Brand new
column17: Made from nothing
column28: Pre- means before, so pre-existing cells are cells that already existed. New cells come from the division of those older cells, not from nothing.
column29: The prefix pre- means before, like in preview or pregame.

column9: A single bacterium divides into 2 cells. Then each of those cells divides, and then each new cell divides one more time. How many cells are there now?
column28: Each round of division doubles the number of cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. A common mistake is adding 2 each round (getting 6) instead of doubling.
column29: Every cell splits into two, so the total doubles each round.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Why do scientists say the cell theory applies to ALL living things?
column14: Cells are found in everything, including rocks and water.
column15: Every kind of organism scientists have examined is made of cells.
column16: Scientists have only studied humans, and humans are made of cells.
column17: A textbook says so, so the idea does not need to be tested.
column28: The cell theory is based on evidence: bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, and animals have all been examined, and every one is made of cells. Rocks and water have no cells, and science relies on evidence, not on a book saying so.
column29: Scientific ideas are supported by evidence. What evidence would show all life has cells?

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: The tissue lining the inside of your mouth is made of what?
column14: Several organs
column15: One giant cell
column16: Atoms but no cells
column17: Many cells working together
column28: A tissue is a group of many similar cells working together. Cells are the building blocks of tissues, and tissues build organs, not the other way around.
column29: Tissues are one level up from cells.

column9: A slice of bread left out on the counter grows fuzzy mold. Where did the mold come from?
column14: Mold spores (tiny cells) from the air landed on the bread and grew.
column15: The bread changed into mold.
column16: Moisture in the bread formed into mold cells.
column17: The air itself turned into mold.
column28: Mold is a living fungus. Its spores float in the air, land on food, and grow by cell division. The bread is food for the mold; it does not turn into mold. Believing it does is the old idea of spontaneous generation.
column29: Mold is alive, so it must come from other living mold.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: An elephant's body cells and a mouse's body cells are about the same size. Why is an elephant so much bigger than a mouse?
column14: It has many more cells.
column15: Its cells are much bigger.
column16: It has fewer, stronger cells.
column17: Its body is not made of cells.
column28: Most body cells are about the same size in big and small animals. An elephant is bigger because it is built from far more cells, which shows that cells are the basic building blocks (units of structure).
column29: The stem says the cells are the same size. So what must be different?

column9: The most common substance in a typical cell, making up about 70% of its mass, is ___.
column28: Cells are about 70% water. Water is part of the similar chemical makeup shared by all cells. A common mistake is answering protein; proteins are the most common large molecule, but there is far more water.
column29: Think of the molecule from Unit 2 that all life needs and that you drink every day.

column9: Robert Hooke saw his first cells in a slice of cork. Where does cork come from?
column14: A type of rock
column15: An animal's skin
column16: A bacterium
column17: The bark of a tree
column28: Cork is the bark of the cork oak tree, so the cells Hooke saw were dead plant cells. Only their walls were left, which is why the boxes looked empty.
column29: Cork stoppers and bulletin boards are made from part of a plant.

column9: Cells on the inside of your cheek are constantly being replaced. According to the cell theory, where do the new cheek cells come from?
column14: Food you eat turning into cells
column15: Existing cheek cells dividing
column16: Saliva forming into cells
column17: Air you breathe in
column28: New cells only come from cells that already exist. Living cells in the cheek lining divide to replace old ones. Food supplies materials, but it does not turn directly into cells.
column29: Every new cell needs a parent cell.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: What does the word multicellular mean?
column14: Made of dead cells only
column15: Made of one cell
column16: Made of no cells
column17: Made of many cells
column28: Multi- means many, so a multicellular organism is made of many cells, like a dog or a tree. Unicellular means one cell, like a bacterium.
column29: Multi- is the same prefix as in multiply or multiple.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Structure means what something is built from. Which observation shows that living things are BUILT from cells?
column14: Onion skin is built from rows of brick-shaped cells.
column15: A nerve cell sends a signal.
column16: A cell breaks down food to release energy.
column17: A cell copies its DNA.
column28: Structure means what something is built from. Onion skin built from rows of cells shows cells as building blocks. The other choices are jobs cells do, which is function, not structure.
column29: Three of the choices describe a job a cell does. One describes what something is made of.

column9: Chloroplasts in a leaf cell capture energy from sunlight and use it to make sugar. Which modern idea of the cell theory does this show?
column14: All living things are made of cells.
column15: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column16: Energy flow happens inside cells.
column17: Cells contain genetic information.
column28: Capturing light energy and storing it in sugar is energy flow, and it happens inside the leaf cell. The other choices are real parts of the cell theory, but this example is about energy.
column29: What is being captured and stored in this example?

column9: A sea star loses an arm to a predator and slowly grows a new one. Where do the cells of the new arm come from?
column14: Sand on the ocean floor
column15: Food that turns directly into arm cells
column16: Cells in the sea star's body that divide
column17: Seawater soaking into the wound
column28: The sea star's own living cells divide again and again to build the new arm. Food gives the energy and materials, but new cells always come from pre-existing cells.
column29: Sand and seawater are not alive. What could make new living cells?

column9: Cells break down which molecule to release the energy they need?
column14: Water
column15: Table salt
column16: Glucose (a sugar)
column17: Carbon dioxide
column28: Cells break down glucose to release energy. Carbon dioxide is a waste that comes out of that process, and water and salt do not provide energy.
column29: It is a carbohydrate from Unit 2 that tastes sweet.

column9: Why does every cell need DNA?
column14: DNA is the cell's main fuel; the cell breaks it down to release energy.
column15: DNA soaks up water and keeps the cell from drying out.
column16: DNA holds the instructions the cell uses to build what it needs, do its work, and divide.
column17: DNA forms the cell's outer wall and gives the cell its shape.
column28: DNA is the cell's set of instructions. It tells the cell which proteins to make and is copied so new cells get the same instructions. Energy comes from food like glucose, not from DNA.
column29: Think of DNA as a recipe book.

column9: Why do cells need a steady supply of energy?
column14: So they can carry out life processes like building molecules, moving materials, and dividing
column15: So they can stop needing food and live on stored energy forever
column16: So they can change into a different kind of organism when conditions change
column17: So they can build new cells out of the nonliving matter around them
column28: Every life process in a cell uses energy, which is why the modern cell theory includes energy flow inside cells. Cells do not change species or form from nonliving matter.
column29: What happens in a cell that would need energy?

column9: Some early scientists, including Schwann, thought new cells formed out of a clear fluid between cells, the way crystals form in a liquid. Rudolf Virchow replaced this idea with which statement?
column14: Cells form only in plants.
column15: New cells form from the food an organism eats.
column16: Cells are made by the heart.
column17: New cells come only from existing cells dividing.
column28: Virchow observed that new cells come from the division of cells that already exist, not from fluid. This became the third part of the cell theory: all cells come from pre-existing cells.
column29: Virchow's famous phrase was every cell from a cell.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Your dog, the grass in your yard, and the bacteria on your skin are very different. Which part of the cell theory do they all show?
column14: All living things are made of one or more cells.
column15: All cells come from food.
column16: Only animals are made of cells.
column17: All cells are the same size.
column28: A dog, grass, and bacteria are all living, so all are made of one or more cells. Grass and bacteria are not animals, and cells come in many sizes.
column29: What do all three have in common because they are alive?

column9: A student says, "My body is made of cells, but my blood isn't. Blood is just a liquid." Which response is correct?
column14: She is wrong; blood contains living cells such as red and white blood cells.
column15: She is right; blood is made only of minerals.
column16: She is wrong; blood is one single giant cell.
column17: She is right; liquids can never contain cells.
column28: Blood is a liquid tissue full of cells: red blood cells carry oxygen and white blood cells fight germs. A common mistake is thinking only solid body parts are made of cells.
column29: What kinds of cells have you heard named after blood?

column9: Put these steps in order to show how one cell becomes two.
column14: The parent cell makes a copy of its DNA
column15: The two new cells grow and can later divide again
column16: The parent cell splits into two new cells, each with one copy of the DNA
column28: The DNA is copied first, so that when the cell splits each new cell gets a full copy. Then the new cells grow. This shows two ideas at once: cells come from pre-existing cells, and genetic information is passed on.
column29: The DNA has to be copied before the cell splits, or one new cell would be left without any.

column9: Match each part of the modern cell theory to the example that shows it.
column14: All living things are made of cells :: A sunflower leaf is built from thousands of cells
column15: All cells come from pre-existing cells :: A puppy grows larger as its cells divide
column16: Cells are the basic unit of structure and function :: Root hair cells soak up water for a plant
column17: Energy flow happens inside cells :: Mitochondria in a heart cell release energy from food
column28: A leaf built of cells shows living things are made of cells. A growing puppy shows new cells come from dividing cells. Root hair cells doing the job of absorbing water show cells are the unit of function. Mitochondria releasing energy shows energy flow happens inside cells.
column29: For each example, ask: is it about what something is made of, where cells come from, a job cells do, or energy?

column9: The original cell theory from the 1800s does not mention DNA. Why not?
column14: DNA is found in only a few kinds of cells.
column15: Cells in the 1800s did not have DNA yet.
column16: The role of DNA as a cell's genetic material was not discovered until the 1900s.
column17: Scientists in the 1800s decided DNA was unimportant.
column28: Scientists showed in the 1940s and 1950s that DNA carries genetic information, and that discovery was added to the modern cell theory. Cells always had DNA; scientists just had not discovered what it does.
column29: Theories grow as new discoveries are made. When was DNA's job figured out?

column9: Robert Hooke named cells, but he never suggested that cells come from other cells. What best explains why?
column14: He thought the cork boxes were air pockets, not parts of a plant.
column15: His microscope was so strong that he could not see whole cells.
column16: He looked at dead cork, so he only saw empty cell walls and never saw cells dividing.
column17: He was not interested in living things, only in building lenses.
column28: Hooke's cork cells were dead and empty, so there was nothing alive to watch divide. That evidence came much later with better microscopes and living samples. Early microscopes were much weaker than modern ones, not stronger.
column29: Think about what you can and can't learn from a dead sample.

column9: A scientist tests an onion skin cell and a bacterium. Both contain proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids. Which idea of the modern cell theory does this support?
column14: All cells have a nucleus.
column15: Cells can form from nonliving material.
column16: All cells have a similar chemical makeup.
column17: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column28: Finding the same four kinds of large molecules in very different cells supports the idea that all cells have a similar chemical makeup. Bacteria have no nucleus, and cells do not form from nonliving material.
column29: The evidence is a list of molecules. Which idea is about what cells are made of chemically?

column9: A jar of grape juice is heated until it boils and is sealed right away. It never ferments until someone opens it. Fermenting requires living yeast cells. What is the best explanation?
column14: Heating killed the yeast, and the seal kept new yeast cells from getting in.
column15: Yeast forms out of juice only when the jar is cold and open.
column16: Opening the jar let in air, and air turns juice into yeast.
column17: Grape juice cannot contain cells, so it can never ferment.
column28: Boiling killed the yeast already in the juice, and the seal kept new yeast out. Once opened, yeast cells from the air or the surroundings got in and multiplied. No yeast ever formed from the juice itself, which supports the idea that cells come only from pre-existing cells.
column29: Two things happened to the jar. What did each one do to the yeast?

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Which of these organisms are unicellular (made of only one cell)? Select all that apply.
column14: Mushroom
column15: Oak tree
column16: Euglena
column17: Earthworm
column28: Paramecium, yeast, and Euglena are each a single cell. Earthworms, oak trees, and mushrooms are multicellular. A common mistake is picking mushroom because it is a fungus like yeast, but a mushroom is made of many cells.
column29: Three of these you would need a microscope to see as a single organism.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: Which of these microscope observations support the idea that all living things are made of cells? Select all that apply.
column14: A drop of pond water shows single-celled algae.
column15: A chip of granite shows mineral crystals.
column16: A thin slice of carrot shows rows of cells.
column17: A slice of frog muscle shows many cells.
column18: A pinch of table salt shows cube-shaped crystals.
column28: The carrot, algae, and frog muscle are living things, and each shows cells. Granite and salt are nonliving, and crystals are not cells, even if salt crystals look like little boxes.
column29: Evidence for this idea must come from living things.

column9: Salt crystals in a dish of salt water slowly grow larger. A student says this proves the crystals are alive. Which response best uses the cell theory?
column14: She is wrong; crystals are not made of cells and do not come from cells, so growing alone does not make them alive.
column15: She is right; anything that grows larger over time must be a living thing.
column16: She is right; each crystal is a single cell that keeps dividing.
column17: She is wrong; crystals are alive only while they are dissolved in water.
column28: Crystals grow by adding more salt to the outside, not by cells dividing. Because crystals are not made of cells, the cell theory says they are not living. A common mistake is using one trait, like growth, to decide something is alive.
column29: What does the cell theory say every living thing must be made of?

column9: The modern cell theory says energy flow happens within cells. All the chemical reactions a cell uses to build up and break down molecules are together called ___.
column28: Metabolism is the total of all chemical reactions in a cell, and many of them move energy around. A common mistake is writing respiration, which is only one part of metabolism.
column29: People say someone has a fast or slow one of these.

column9: A student wants to test whether microbes can appear in broth without coming from other cells. Which experiment design is best?
column14: Boil two flasks of broth, seal one and leave the other open, and check which one grows microbes.
column15: Boil one flask of broth and taste it after a week to see if it spoiled.
column16: Leave one unboiled flask open and see whether microbes appear in it.
column17: Weigh one flask of broth every day to see if it gains mass.
column28: Boiling both flasks kills any microbes already there. Sealing only one makes contact with the air the only difference, so the open flask is the comparison. One flask alone has no comparison, and weighing or tasting does not test for microbes.
column29: A good experiment changes only one thing between two groups.

column9: A wooden desk is made of the walls of dead plant cells. A student says, "The desk is made of cells, so it must be alive." What is wrong with this reasoning?
column14: Only animal cells can be alive, so a plant product never could be.
column15: Wood has never contained cells; it is made of minerals from the soil.
column16: Nothing is wrong; anything that is made of cells is alive.
column17: The desk's cells are dead and can no longer carry out life processes, so the desk is not alive.
column28: The cell theory says living things are made of cells, but that does not mean everything with cells is alive now. Wood came from living tree cells, and those cells are now dead. Plant cells are just as alive as animal cells while the plant lives.
column29: Was the wood ever alive? Is it alive now?

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: A ribosome is one tiny part inside a cell. Why isn't a ribosome by itself considered alive?
column14: It is too large to be alive; living things must be smaller than organelles.
column15: It has no atoms in it, so it cannot be made of matter.
column16: It is made only of water and salt, which are nonliving.
column17: It is only one part of a cell and cannot carry out all life processes on its own.
column28: The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out every life process. A ribosome only builds proteins; it cannot take in energy, respond, or reproduce by itself. That is why the cell, not its parts, is the basic unit of life.
column29: Compare one part of a factory to the whole factory.

column9: Robert Hooke described cells in 1665. Rudolf Virchow stated that all cells come from pre-existing cells in 1855. How many years passed between these two events?
column28: 1855 − 1665 = 190 years. The cell theory was built slowly over nearly two centuries by many scientists. A common mistake is subtracting the wrong way or mixing up the digits.
column29: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.

column9: A student says, "The cell theory says all cells have a similar chemical makeup, so all cells must look the same." What is the best correction?
column14: The student is right; similar chemistry means every cell looks exactly alike.
column15: Cells are made of the same kinds of molecules, but they can be very different in shape and size, like long nerve cells and round egg cells.
column16: Only plant cells have a similar makeup, because only plants have cell walls.
column17: Cells are made of different kinds of molecules, but every cell has the same shape.
column28: Similar chemical makeup means the same kinds of molecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids), not the same shape. Nerve cells can be very long and egg cells are round, but both are built from the same kinds of molecules.
column29: Chemical makeup is about what cells are made of, not what they look like.

column9: A poison stops a cell from releasing energy from its food. What will most likely happen to the cell?
column14: It will turn into a nonliving crystal.
column15: It will divide more often.
column16: It will grow faster.
column17: It will stop carrying out life processes and die.
column28: Every life process in a cell, from building molecules to dividing, needs energy. Without energy flow inside the cell, those processes stop and the cell dies. It cannot grow or divide without energy.
column29: What does a cell need energy for?

column9: A robot vacuum moves around a room, senses walls, and uses energy from its battery. Using the cell theory, why is it NOT alive?
column14: It is too noisy.
column15: It does not move.
column16: It uses energy.
column17: It is not made of cells.
column28: The robot moves, senses, and uses energy, but it is not made of cells, so by the cell theory it is not a living thing. Using energy and moving are traits of life, but they are not enough without cells.
column29: Look for the one requirement of the cell theory the robot fails.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Put these levels of organization in order from smallest to largest.
column14: Cell
column15: Tissue
column16: Molecule
column17: Atom
column28: Atoms join to make molecules, molecules build cells, cells form tissues, and tissues form organs. The cell is the first level that is alive, which is why it is the basic unit of life. A common mistake is putting molecule after cell.
column29: Start with the smallest particle of matter, and remember that the cell is the first living level.

column9: A classmate's study guide lists these "facts" about the cell theory. Which ones are mistakes that do NOT belong? Select all that apply.
column14: All living things are made of one or more cells.
column15: Cells contain genetic information.
column16: All cells are the same size.
column17: All cells contain chloroplasts.
column18: New cells can be made from the food you eat.
column28: Cells come only from pre-existing cells, not from food. Only some plant and algae cells have chloroplasts, and cells come in many sizes. Genetic information and "all living things are made of cells" ARE part of the cell theory.
column29: Find the statements that are false. Careful: you are choosing the ones that do NOT belong.

column4: All living things are made of cells
column9: The first evidence for the cell theory came from plants and animals. Which pair of organisms would give the strongest NEW evidence that the cell theory applies to all life, not just plants and animals?
column14: A bacterium and a mushroom
column15: An oak tree and a robin
column16: A dog and a cat
column17: A rose and a tulip
column28: A bacterium and a mushroom are neither plants nor animals, so finding cells in them extends the theory to new groups of life. The other pairs are plants, animals, or one of each, which only repeats the earliest evidence.
column29: Which pair has no plants and no animals in it?

column9: Your bone marrow makes about 2 million new red blood cells every second. According to the cell theory, where do these new cells come from?
column14: Cells in the bone marrow that divide
column15: Iron in your food forming into cells
column16: Oxygen from your lungs
column17: Blood plasma clumping together
column28: Cells inside the bone marrow keep dividing to make new blood cells. Iron and oxygen are used by red blood cells, but they do not become cells. New cells always come from pre-existing cells.
column29: Iron, plasma, and oxygen are not cells. What could make a new cell?

column9: Leeuwenhoek called the tiny living things he saw swimming in pond water "___," a word that means little animals.
column28: Leeuwenhoek called them animalcules (little animals). Today we know they were single-celled organisms such as protists and bacteria. They showed that one cell can be a whole living thing.
column29: It starts with animal and ends with a word part that means small.

column9: A scientist grows a single carrot cell in a dish of nutrients. It divides again and again until it becomes a whole new carrot plant. Which idea does this show most directly?
column14: Cells form from the nutrients in the dish, because the dish has everything a cell is made of.
column15: Plants are not made of cells, because one cell turned into a whole plant.
column16: All cells come from pre-existing cells, because every cell in the new plant came from the first cell.
column17: Cells cannot divide outside an organism, so the plant must have grown from soil.
column28: Every cell in the new plant traces back to the one starting cell, which shows new cells come from pre-existing cells. The nutrients are food for the cells; they do not become new cells by themselves.
column29: Trace where each new cell came from.

column9: Long ago, people saw mice appear in barns full of stored grain and concluded that grain turns into mice. What is the better explanation?
column14: Mice came in from outside and had babies; living things come from other living things.
column15: Mice form out of barn dust.
column16: Grain really does turn into mice in the dark.
column17: Mice can only form in the winter.
column28: The belief that grain turns into mice is spontaneous generation, which was disproved. Mice came from parent mice that got into the barn to eat the grain. Grain is food, not a source of new life.
column29: Grain is what mice eat. Why would mice show up where there is food?

column9: Which of these are examples of energy flow happening inside cells? Select all that apply.
column14: A cell using energy to build proteins
column15: Wind spinning a windmill
column16: A cell breaking down food molecules to release energy
column17: A white blood cell using energy to crawl toward bacteria
column28: Breaking down food, building proteins, and moving all involve energy flow inside living cells. A river and the wind move energy too, but they are not cells, so they are not examples of this part of the cell theory.
column29: Pick only the examples that happen inside a cell.

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Red blood cells carry oxygen, nerve cells send signals, and muscle cells contract. How does this support the idea that cells are the basic unit of function?
column14: It shows that organs, not cells, do all of the body's work.
column15: It shows that all cells are identical, since each one does a job.
column16: It shows that cells come from nonliving matter inside each organ.
column17: Each job the body does is carried out by cells built for that job.
column28: Different cells do different jobs, and together those jobs keep you alive. That means life's functions happen at the level of cells. Organs work only because the cells in them do their jobs.
column29: Notice that each example is a cell doing something.

column9: Bacteria contain DNA even though they have no nucleus.
column28: True. Bacteria are prokaryotic cells with no nucleus, but their DNA floats in the cytoplasm. The modern cell theory says all cells contain genetic information, nucleus or not.
column29: Does a cell need a nucleus to have genetic information?

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Doctors often look at a small sample of cells (a biopsy) under a microscope to diagnose a disease. Why does this make sense based on the cell theory?
column14: Because only dead cells can be seen under a microscope.
column15: Because the body's work is done by cells, many diseases show up as changes in cells.
column16: Because most diseases are caused by nonliving matter that collects between cells.
column17: Because cells never change, so any cell sample will look healthy.
column28: If cells are the basic unit of structure and function, then when something goes wrong in the body, it often shows up in the cells. Doctors check cells for changes in shape, size, or number.
column29: If cells do the body's work, where would a problem show up?

column4: Cell theory as a scientific theory
column9: Robert Hooke published detailed drawings of what he saw in a 1665 book. Why did publishing his observations matter for building the cell theory?
column14: It kept other scientists from studying cells.
column15: It proved the whole cell theory by itself.
column16: It showed that cells come from cork.
column17: It let other scientists check his work and build on it.
column28: Science grows when scientists share their findings. Hooke's book let others repeat his observations and look for cells in other living things. No single book proved the whole theory; it took many scientists.
column29: How do other scientists learn about a discovery?

column9: In Unit 2 you learned the elements CHNOPS. How do these elements support one part of the modern cell theory?
column14: They prove all cells are the same size.
column15: They make up most of the molecules in every cell, which shows all cells have a similar chemical makeup.
column16: They are found only in plant cells.
column17: They show that all cells come from rocks.
column28: Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur build the large molecules in every cell, from bacteria to people. That shared chemistry supports the idea that all cells have a similar chemical makeup.
column29: Which part of the cell theory is about what cells are made of?

column9: Scientists can insert the human gene for insulin into a bacterium. The bacterium then reads the gene and makes human insulin. Which idea of the modern cell theory does this support most directly?
column14: All living things are made of one or more cells.
column15: All cells store genetic information in DNA and read it in a similar way.
column16: All cells are the same size, so a gene fits in any cell.
column17: Cells can form from nonliving material when given the right gene.
column28: A bacterium can read a human gene because both kinds of cells use DNA as genetic information in the same basic way. "All living things are made of cells" is true, but it does not explain why a human gene works in a bacterium.
column29: Why would a bacterium be able to understand a human gene at all?

column9: A scientist fills a sterile dish with every chemical found inside a cell: water, proteins, lipids, sugars, and DNA. No living cells are added. According to the cell theory, what will happen?
column14: No new cell will form, because cells come only from pre-existing cells.
column15: A new cell will assemble from the chemicals within a few days.
column16: Only bacteria will form, since they are the simplest cells.
column17: Many cells will form if the dish is kept warm.
column28: Having the right ingredients is not enough. The cell theory says new cells come only from existing cells, which have the organized structure needed to make more cells. A common mistake is thinking warmth or time will make life appear.
column29: Is there a parent cell in the dish?

column9: E. coli bacteria can divide every 20 minutes. If you start with 1 E. coli cell, how many cells will there be after 2 hours, assuming every cell keeps dividing?
column28: 2 hours = 120 minutes, and 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. The number doubles each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64. A common mistake is multiplying 6 × 2 = 12 instead of doubling six times.
column29: First find how many 20-minute periods fit in 2 hours. Then double that many times.

column9: A student counts yeast cells in a flask of sugar water: 100 cells at 0 hours, 200 at 2 hours, 400 at 4 hours, and 800 at 6 hours. Which conclusion best fits the data and the cell theory?
column14: The yeast cells are getting bigger, not more numerous.
column15: Each existing yeast cell divides, so the number doubles about every 2 hours.
column16: The number of cells will stay at 800 from now on.
column17: New yeast cells form from the sugar water, about 100 every 2 hours.
column28: The count doubles every 2 hours, which is what happens when every existing cell divides. If cells formed from sugar water at a steady rate, the count would go up by the same amount each time, not double. The data count cells, so the number is growing, not just the size.
column29: Is the count going up by the same amount each time, or by the same factor?

column9: Pasteur boiled broth in a swan-neck flask that was open to the air, and the broth stayed clear for months. Then he tipped the flask so the broth flowed up into the bend of the neck and back. Soon the broth turned cloudy with microbes. What does this result show?
column14: Tipping the flask let warm air into the broth, and warmth turns broth into microbes.
column15: Microbes came from cells that had collected in the bend of the neck, not from the broth itself.
column16: Moving any liquid causes new life to form from the liquid itself.
column17: The broth turned into microbes once it was moved, because moving it mixed in oxygen.
column28: Dust carrying microbes from the air was trapped in the curved neck. When broth touched that dust, the microbes got in and multiplied. The broth sat open to air for months without growing anything, so it was not making life on its own. This supports the idea that cells come only from pre-existing cells.
column29: Something was waiting in the bend of the neck. What could have been trapped there from the air?

column9: A student sets up four jars of broth and leaves them for a week. Jar A: boiled, then sealed. Jar B: boiled, then left open. Jar C: not boiled, then sealed. Jar D: not boiled, then left open. Which jars will most likely turn cloudy with microbes?
column14: Only D
column15: B and D only
column16: B, C, and D
column17: All four jars
column28: Jar A is the only one with no living microbes inside and no way for new ones to get in. B was open, so microbes got in from the air. C was sealed, but it was never boiled, so the microbes already in it multiplied. A common mistake is thinking a seal alone keeps broth clear.
column29: For each jar, ask: were microbes killed, and could new ones get in?

column4: Cells are the basic unit of life
column9: Which observations support the idea that cells are the basic unit of function? Select all that apply.
column14: White blood cells surround and destroy bacteria.
column15: Minerals in a rock line up in layers.
column16: Cells in the pancreas release insulin into the blood.
column17: Cells in the stomach lining release acid that helps digest food.
column18: Wind carries dandelion seeds across a field.
column28: Releasing insulin, releasing stomach acid, and destroying bacteria are jobs done by cells, which shows cells are the unit of function. Rock layers and wind are nonliving processes. Seeds are made of cells, but the wind, not the seeds' cells, is doing the work.
column29: In each choice, ask: is a cell the one doing the job?

column9: Researchers find a tiny particle in a hot spring. It contains DNA and protein but has no cell membrane, and it can only make copies of itself inside bacteria. How should it be classified using the cell theory?
column14: As a new kind of bacterium, because it lives in a hot spring like many bacteria
column15: As proof that cells can form from nonliving matter in hot water
column16: As not a living cell; like a virus, it is not made of a cell and needs a host cell to copy itself
column17: As a living cell, because anything with DNA and protein counts as a cell
column28: Having DNA is not enough to be a living cell. The particle has no membrane, so it is not a cell, and it depends on bacteria to copy itself, just like a virus. It does not form from nonliving matter; it is copied inside living cells.
column29: Does it meet the cell theory's requirement for a living thing?

column9: Rudolf Virchow argued that diseases like cancer begin with changes in the body's own cells. How does this connect to his idea that every cell comes from a cell?
column14: It shows that tumors form from nonliving matter that builds up in the body.
column15: If every cell comes from a cell, tumor cells must come from the patient's own cells dividing out of control.
column16: It shows that cancer cells come straight from the food a person eats.
column17: It shows that tumors are not made of cells, so his idea does not apply to them.
column28: A tumor is a mass of cells, and by Virchow's rule those cells came from earlier cells: the patient's own cells that began dividing out of control. Tumors are made of cells, and they do not form from food or nonliving matter.
column29: Apply every cell from a cell to the cells in a tumor.

column9: Match each piece of evidence to the part of the cell theory it supports best.
column14: Frog skin, frog muscle, and frog blood all turn out to be built from cells :: All living things are made of cells
column15: A kidney cleans the blood because its cells filter out wastes :: Cells are the basic unit of structure and function
column16: Boiled, sealed broth never grows microbes :: All cells come from pre-existing cells
column17: A bacterium's offspring have the same traits as the parent :: Cells contain genetic information passed on during division
column28: The frog is a living thing built from cells. The kidney's work is done by its cells, which shows function. Sealed, boiled broth stays clear because no cells are there to make new ones. Offspring with the parent's traits show DNA is passed on during division.
column29: Decide what each piece of evidence is about: what life is made of, a job, where cells come from, or traits.

column9: A sample from a pond is described as alive. Which findings would support that claim using the cell theory? Select all that apply.
column14: It contains the same molecules as living things but has no cells.
column15: It grows by adding layers of crystals to its surface.
column16: Its cells contain DNA.
column17: New cells appear only when its existing cells divide.
column18: It is made of one or more cells.
column28: Being made of cells, having DNA, and making new cells only by division all fit the cell theory. Growing by adding crystals is how nonliving crystals grow, and having life's molecules without any cells is not enough to be alive.
column29: Each correct finding should match a part of the cell theory.

column9: Put the steps of Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment in order.
column14: Pour broth into a flask with a long, S-shaped neck
column15: Tip the flask so the broth flows into the bend of the neck and back, then watch for microbes
column16: Let the flask sit open to the air for weeks and see that the broth stays clear
column17: Boil the broth to kill any microbes
column28: Broth goes in first, then it is boiled to kill microbes. Next, the open flask sits for weeks to show broth alone does not make life. Last, tipping the flask lets the broth touch what is trapped in the neck, and microbes grow. A common mistake is putting the tipping step before the waiting step.
column29: You must kill the microbes before you can test whether new ones appear.

column9: Put these events in the history of the cell theory in order, from earliest to latest.
column14: Scientists discover that DNA carries a cell's genetic information
column15: Hooke names cells after looking at cork
column16: Leeuwenhoek sees living single-celled organisms
column17: Schleiden and Schwann conclude that living things are made of cells
column18: Virchow states that all cells come from pre-existing cells
column28: Hooke (1665) came first, then Leeuwenhoek (1670s), Schleiden and Schwann (1838–1839), Virchow (1855), and finally the discovery of DNA's role (1900s). A common mistake is putting Virchow before Schleiden and Schwann.
column29: The DNA discovery is the most recent. Hooke is the earliest.

column9: In the 1740s, John Needham boiled broth briefly, corked the flasks, and later found microbes growing. He decided life formed from the broth. Later, Lazzaro Spallanzani boiled broth longer and melted the glass necks shut, and no microbes grew. What best explains Needham's results?
column14: Needham's broth had no nutrients in it.
column15: Spallanzani's flasks had no air, and microbes form out of air.
column16: His broth was not boiled long enough or sealed tightly enough, so living microbes survived or got in.
column17: Life really does form from broth, but only in corked flasks.
column28: Spallanzani showed that with longer boiling and a tight seal, nothing grew. So Needham's microbes were living cells that survived the short boil or got past the cork. Microbes do not form out of air; they travel in air on dust.
column29: Compare the two methods. What did Spallanzani do differently?

column9: A student wants to show that mold doesn't come from the bread itself. She seals one slice of store-bought bread in a bag and leaves another slice open on the counter. After a week, BOTH slices grow mold. What is the most likely reason the sealed slice grew mold?
column14: Mold forms out of the plastic bag.
column15: The sealed bread turned into mold.
column16: Mold spores were already on the bread before it was sealed.
column17: Sealing bread speeds up spontaneous generation.
column28: Mold spores are everywhere, so they were likely on the bread before it went into the bag. Sealing kept new spores out but did not kill the ones already there. To fix the experiment, she would need to kill the spores first. Spontaneous generation has been disproved.
column29: Sealing keeps things out. Did it remove anything already inside?

column9: Virchow published his idea that all cells come from cells in 1855, but many people still believed microbes could form from broth until Pasteur's experiments around 1860. Why was Pasteur's work still important?
column14: It showed that plants are made of cells, which Virchow had never studied.
column15: It gave clear experimental evidence that microbes come only from other microbes, not from nonliving broth.
column16: It proved that Virchow was wrong about where new cells come from.
column17: It showed for the first time that cells contain DNA, which Virchow did not know.
column28: Virchow's idea was based mostly on studying cells in tissues. Pasteur's controlled experiments tested spontaneous generation directly for microbes and supported Virchow. Pasteur did not study DNA, and plant cells had been described decades earlier.
column29: An idea becomes stronger when an experiment tests it directly.

column4: Cell theory as a scientific theory
column9: After looking at onion skin cells one time, a student writes, "All living things are made of cells." What is the biggest weakness in how she reached this conclusion?
column14: One sample from one organism is not enough evidence for a claim about all living things.
column15: Onion cells are too small to count.
column16: Onions are not living things.
column17: She should have used a telescope instead.
column28: A claim about ALL living things needs evidence from many kinds of organisms. That is why the cell theory took the work of many scientists studying plants, animals, and microbes. Her conclusion happens to be right, but her evidence is too thin to support it.
column29: How much evidence do you need to make a claim about every living thing?

column9: A scientist removes the nucleus from a cell of one kind of single-celled organism (Type A) and puts in a nucleus from Type B. Later the cell divides, and the new cells have the traits of Type B. What does this show?
column14: The cell's traits come only from the cytoplasm, which still came from Type A.
column15: The new cells formed from nonliving matter inside the old cell.
column16: Cells do not need DNA to divide, because the new cells formed anyway.
column17: The cell's traits are controlled by the genetic information in the nucleus, and that information is passed on when the cell divides.
column28: The new cells matched the nucleus, not the rest of the cell, so the DNA in the nucleus controls the traits and is passed on during division. If the cytoplasm controlled traits, the new cells would look like Type A.
column29: Which part of the cell came from Type B, and which traits did the new cells have?

column9: A student makes these claims. Which are consistent with the modern cell theory? Select all that apply.
column14: A muscle cell and a bacterium are built from similar kinds of molecules.
column15: The cells lining my stomach came from earlier stomach cells that divided.
column16: New bacteria can form from spoiled food.
column17: The yeast in my bread dough contains DNA.
column18: A campfire is alive because it grows and uses oxygen.
column28: Cells come from dividing cells, all cells contain DNA, and all cells share a similar chemical makeup. A fire is not made of cells, so it is not alive even though it grows. Bacteria come from other bacteria, not from food.
column29: Check each claim against one part of the cell theory.

column9: A cell divides every 30 minutes, and every new cell keeps dividing at the same rate. Starting from 1 cell, how many rounds of division does it take to reach at least 1,000 cells?
column28: Keep doubling: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 after 9 rounds, then 1,024 after 10 rounds. Nine rounds gives only 512, so it takes 10. A common mistake is dividing 1,000 by 2 and answering 500.
column29: Count how many times you have to double 1 to pass 1,000.

column9: Four samples are tested. W: made of cells, contains DNA, cells divide. X: not made of cells, contains DNA, copies itself only inside a host cell. Y: not made of cells, no DNA, grows by adding layers. Z: made of cells, contains DNA, cells divide slowly. Which samples are living organisms according to the cell theory?
column14: W only
column15: W and Z
column16: X and Y
column17: All four
column28: W and Z are made of cells that contain DNA and divide, so both are living. Dividing slowly does not make Z nonliving. X acts like a virus and Y acts like a crystal; neither is made of cells.
column29: The first test is whether the sample is made of cells.

column9: Scientists can make tiny bubbles of fat in water. The bubbles form on their own, and some even split in two when shaken. Does this go against the cell theory?
column14: No; the bubbles have no DNA and cannot carry out life processes, so they are not living cells.
column15: Yes; anything that splits in two on its own counts as a dividing cell.
column16: Yes; the bubbles prove that cells can form from nonliving matter.
column17: No; the bubbles are actually tiny bacteria that were already in the water.
column28: A fat bubble may look a little like a cell membrane, but it has no DNA, no energy flow, and cannot carry out life processes. Splitting when shaken is not the same as cell division. So it is not a cell, and the cell theory still holds.
column29: Does a bubble have the other things the modern cell theory says every cell has?

column9: Every one of the trillions of cells in your body came from earlier cells. If you trace that chain of cell divisions back, where does it start?
column14: With your heart cells
column15: With cells formed from the food your mother ate
column16: With cells formed from nonliving matter at birth
column17: With a single fertilized egg cell
column28: You began as one fertilized egg cell, which formed when an egg cell and a sperm cell joined. That one cell divided again and again to make every cell in your body. Food supplied materials, but it never turned directly into cells.
column29: How many cells were you made of at the very beginning?

column9: Plant cells have cell walls and chloroplasts, but animal cells do not. A student says this proves the cell theory's idea of a similar chemical makeup is wrong. What is the best response?
column14: Animal cells have hidden chloroplasts, so the two kinds of cells are really the same.
column15: Cells can have different parts and still be built from the same kinds of molecules and use DNA, so the idea still holds.
column16: The student is right; plant and animal cells are built from completely different molecules.
column17: Cell walls are nonliving, so plants are not truly made of cells.
column28: Similar chemical makeup means all cells are built from the same kinds of molecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids). Plant and animal cells have some different parts, but those parts are made of the same kinds of molecules.
column29: Having different parts is not the same as being made of different kinds of molecules.

column9: A student puts live yeast in a sealed jar of sugar water next to a sealed jar of sugar water with no yeast. Only the jar with yeast fills with carbon dioxide bubbles. What does this best show?
column14: Carbon dioxide is alive, because it bubbles and moves around the jar.
column15: Yeast forms out of sugar water when it is kept warm and sealed.
column16: Energy flow happens inside living cells: the yeast cells break down sugar and release carbon dioxide.
column17: Sugar water gives off carbon dioxide on its own once the jar is sealed.
column28: The jar without yeast is the control, and it made no gas, so the sugar water did not make carbon dioxide on its own. The yeast cells broke down sugar for energy and gave off carbon dioxide, which shows energy flow happens inside cells.
column29: Compare the two jars. What is the only difference between them?
